git commit -q -F - <<'MSG'
perf(io): fgets() read ONE BYTE per read(2) — 538 ms where php takes 4

A read request can tell its source how many bytes it wants. A LINE read cannot:
it does not know how many there are until it finds the newline. So `__rt_fgets`
asked the descriptor for one byte, scanned it, and asked again — one `read(2)`
per byte of the file. MEASURED over a 900 KB file of 100 000 lines:

    php -n 8.5.6      4 ms
    elephc          538 ms

php never asks a file for the bytes a caller wanted either; it asks for a whole
CHUNK and keeps the surplus in the stream's own read buffer. That buffer already
exists here — `__rt_fread` fills it, and `unread_bytes` reports it — but nothing
filled it on a line read, so the holding area was empty every time `fgets()`
looked, and the loop fell through to the descriptor for the next single byte.

`__rt_stream_pending_fill(handle)` is the missing half: read one chunk, hand the
whole thing to the stream, take nothing back. `__rt_fgets` calls it when nothing
is held, then scans the held bytes WHERE THEY LIE and takes the whole line out in
one `__rt_stream_pending_consume(handle, n)`. Same file: 20 ms.

A fill that buffers nothing — a pipe, a failed read, end of file — answers 0 and
falls straight through to the single-byte read, so every EOF and errno answer
stays exactly where it was. `S_ISREG` gates it, as it does for `__rt_fread`:
reading ahead on a socket changes when a read blocks, which is a separate
question. EOF is the CALLER's question, so a fill that produced bytes clears the
end-of-file `__rt_fread` set against the chunk IT asked for.

Filling the holding area on a line read exposed the one consumer that was still
blind to it. `stream_get_line()` drained it in BULK, straight into the result
window, past the delimiter scan — which lives behind the per-byte door:

    $h = fopen('data://text/plain,abcdef', 'r');
    fgets($h, 4);                          // abc, leaving def held
    stream_get_line($h, 1024, 'ef');       // php: d      elephc: def

Held bytes now arrive through the same door as descriptor bytes, so each one
meets the tail comparison — which is also what makes a delimiter STRADDLING the
holding area and the descriptor match at all. It is strictly safer than the bulk
drain it replaces: a would-block refusal now puts bytes back only when nothing is
still held, where before it could free a partially drained buffer.

Verified: the 183-program round-8 corpus is unchanged at 180 identical, and the
three that differ are the three that already did. 1088 `io::` tests, 272 `spl::`,
50 csv and 1532 unit tests pass. `tests/codegen/io/line_reads.rs` pins a line that
SPANS several chunks, the positions and `unread_bytes` around a fill, and both
`stream_get_line()` cases, each measured on `php -n` 8.5.6.
